newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian judge has no regrets over Priebke verdict.
newsitem.headline: Italian judge has no regrets over Priebke verdict.

text.p: The military judge who presided over the war crimes trial of former SS captain Erich Priebke said on Wednesday he had no regrets about his handling of the case despite a stunning appeal court decision to order a re-trial.

Agostino Quistelli headed a panel of three judges which in August found Priebke guilty of multiple murder in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, but freed him because of mitigating circumstances and a statute of limitations.

The Court of Cassation on Tuesday annulled the controversial verdict and ordered that 83-year old Priebke, who is being held in a jail in central Rome, should face a fresh trial over the SS reprisal execution of 335 men and boys in 1944.

"I wouldn't change a comma of what I did," Quistelli told La Repubblica newspaper in an interview. "I tried an old man who represents no danger to society, who committed a crime more than half a century ago," he added.

The Court of Cassation did not rule on the verdict itself, but instead overturned a lower appeal court's decision dating from July which had rejected accusations that Quistelli was biased in favour of the accused.

News of a re-trial was greeted with relief by the relatives of the people killed in the massacre, carried out at the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome. Newspapers said Italy must not squander this latest opportunity to confront its past.

"We expect a just sentence which once and for all will put an end to this terrible chapter of our recent history," La Stampa newspaper said in an editorial. "No-one wants vendettas, but no-one expects easy pardons."
However some feared that Priebke, who lived openly for almost 50 years in Argentina before being brought to Italy for trial, could not now receive a fair hearing.
"They are doing all they can to make sure that Priebke dies in prison," said military judge Bruno Rocchi, who sat alongside Quistelli on the bench in the original trial.
One of Priebke's lawyers said he wanted house arrest for his client and accused politicians of interfering in the case.
"This is a fine example of political justice," defence lawyer Carlo Taormina told Corriere della Sera newspaper.

Priebke went on trial amidst a blaze of publicity on May 8, accused of complicity over the slayings. He admitted shooting two people and checking off names from a list at the caves, but his lawyers argued he should not be held responsible because he had to follow orders.
The chaotic proceedings, which at times bordered on farce, ended in a 2-1 verdict to release Priebke.

The convoluted ruling drew swift condemnation from around the world and Priebke himself was besieged inside the courthouse by angry protesters. He was re-arrested hours later when Germany said it intended to extradite him for a war crimes trial there.
Antonino Intelisano, who prosecuted Priebke, has said the German extradition request must now wait and indicated that the re-trial could take place within three or four months.
